outcome: No event dated after 26 January 2024 settles or moves the d≥3 question. The older Durand-Lose (2001) composition theorem is read by some sources as answering it for every dimension and by others (Wikipedia's reversible CA article, Arrighi and Nesme 2010) as leaving it open, because of an enlarged-alphabet caveat I could not resolve from the full text; Wikipedia's article still lists the d≥3 case as open as of 12 October 2026.
problem_asks: (1) For every dimension d ≥ 3 (each d is a separate sub-case, so infinitely many). (2) The class: every reversible cellular automaton of that dimension, i.e. a CA whose global map on configurations is a bijection (for finite-state CA, equivalently injective). (3) The property: 'locally reversible', which the statement does not define. The Wikipedia article and its sources read it as: the CA's update can be carried out by a reversible local rule, e.g. a composition of block permutations / an array of reversible gates on a partition of the lattice, with the same automaton and (on the strict reading) the same state set and neighbourhood, as opposed to a simulation of it by a different automaton with more states. (4) The question is yes/no: is every such automaton locally reversible? A positive answer for all d ≥ 3 settles it; a single non-locally-reversible reversible CA in some d ≥ 3 would refute it.

events.what_happened: Toffoli and Margolus, 'Invertible cellular automata: a review', Physica D 45 (1990) 229–253 (DOI 10.1016/0167-2789(90)90185-R). Per Wikipedia's reversible CA article, they were the first to ask whether every reversible cellular automaton has a locally reversible update rule. This event is the posing of the question, with no result attached. I could not read the paper: the MIT CSAIL PDF returns scanned page images through my fetch tool. Culik (1987) reports, in a search summary of its abstract, that Toffoli and Margolus posed the separate problem of testing whether a rule has an inverse, decidable in 1D and open in higher dimensions; that is a different question.
events.delivers: None. Poses the question; establishes nothing about it.
events.direction: Not a result. It is the source of the yes/no question whose d ≥ 3 case is at issue.

events.what_happened: Kari, 'Representation of reversible cellular automata with block permutations', Mathematical Systems Theory 29(1) (1996) 47–61 (DOI 10.1007/BF01201813). Wikipedia's reversible CA article states that Kari (1996) showed the answer to the locally reversible question is positive for one- and two-dimensional automata. Arrighi and Nesme (arXiv 1201.5529, abstract opened; full text not readable) describe Kari's result as: every one- or two-dimensional reversible CA is a composition of finite reversible gates ('block permutations') and partial shifts, with three layers needed in 2D. The Springer page redirected to a login and I did not open Kari's paper, so both descriptions are secondary.
events.delivers: For d = 1 and d = 2 only: every reversible CA is a composition of block permutations and partial shifts (secondary descriptions). Says nothing for d ≥ 3.
events.remains: Every part of problem_asks for d ≥ 3.
events.direction: Positive, for d = 1 and d = 2 (cuts toward yes in those dimensions only).

events.what_happened: Kari, 'On the circuit depth of structurally reversible cellular automata', Fundamenta Informaticae 38(1–2) (1999) 93–107 (DOI 10.3233/FI-1999-381208). I did not open the paper: the oadoi/unpaywall redirect was not followed. A search-result summary of the IOS Press record reports: (a) every reversible CA can be embedded into the standard two-layer Margolus neighbourhood using two one-to-one local rules, allowing step-by-step simulation; (b) in d dimensions any d+2 consecutive layers of local rules can be combined into d+1, so d+1 layers always suffice; (c) in two dimensions d+1 = 3 is tight, with an example of a three-layer reversible CA that cannot be written with two layers. Arrighi and Nesme (arXiv 1201.5529) cite Kari 1999 for the layer story, according to a search summary I did not verify.
events.delivers: Per the unopened summary: a layer-count bound of d+1 layers in every dimension d for decompositions into one-to-one local rules, plus an embedding (simulation) of any reversible CA in a two-layer Margolus neighbourhood. Whether the layers act on the same alphabet and are the automaton's own rule, rather than a simulation, is not established from anything I could read.
events.remains: Whether the d+1 layered form for d ≥ 3 keeps the given automaton's state set and rule (no added states or coding). Not established from the summary.
events.direction: Leans toward yes in the layered sense for every d (d+1 layers suffice), if the summary is accurate; tight at d = 2.
events.object: A three-layer two-dimensional reversible CA that cannot be written as a two-layer one (per the unopened summary). It shows the layer count d+1 is optimal in 2D; it is not a counterexample to local reversibility, since three layers of one-to-one rules are themselves locally reversible.

events.what_happened: Durand-Lose, 'Representing Reversible Cellular Automata with Reversible Block Cellular Automata', DMTCS Proceedings AA (DM-CCG 2001), pp. 145–154 (DOI 10.46298/dmtcs.2297). The DMTCS abstract page (opened) gives 'Published on December 31, 2000' for a volume labelled DM-CCG 2001. Abstract, quoted: 'We prove that any d-dimensional reversible cellular automaton can be expressed as the composition of d+1 block permutations.' It adds: 'This proves a 1990 conjecture by Toffoli and Margolus (Physica D 45) improved by Kari in 1996 (Mathematical System Theory 29).' It also states: 'We built a simulation in linear time of reversible cellular automata by reversible block cellular automata', valid for finite and infinite configurations. The full PDF returns raw compressed bytes through my tools and the HAL copy was blocked by a bot check, so I could not read the body, the definition of block permutation, or whether the composition keeps the alphabet. Wikipedia's reversible CA article paraphrases the paper as showing that any reversible CA 'could be simulated by a (possibly different) locally reversible cellular automaton', and Wikipedia's block CA article says the simulation uses 'a larger number of states'. Arrighi and Nesme (2010) say the depth-(d+1) block simulation works 'by increasing the size of the alphabet'.
events.revisions: DMTCS page date 31 Dec 2000 for a proceedings volume dated 2001; no later version found.
events.delivers: Per the abstract: for every d (including every d ≥ 3), any d-dimensional reversible CA is expressed as a composition of d+1 block permutations, and reversible CA are simulated linear-time by reversible block CA. Whether the composition is an identity of the same automaton's global map on the same alphabet and neighbourhood, or only a simulation with more states, is not stated in the abstract and I could not check the text. The abstract does not define 'locally reversible'.
events.remains: On the strict reading (same alphabet, the automaton's own update rule), Arrighi and Nesme (2010) say the d ≥ 3 case is open, and Wikipedia's reversible CA article says so too. On the composition reading, nothing in the statement's words remains open for any d. Which reading is correct depends on the full text.

checked_by.qualification: Researchers on reversible and block cellular automata; authors of the two Arrighi–Nesme papers recorded here
checked_by.what_they_did: Cite Durand-Lose 2001 and the Kari results; state that the depth-(d+1) block representation with no extra space or coding is known for d = 1 and 2 and is 'still an open problem' for higher dimensions. They do not claim to have verified Durand-Lose's proof.

events.direction: Toward yes: the abstract says every d-dimensional reversible CA is expressible as a composition of d+1 block permutations, for every d ≥ 3 included. Whether that counts as the statement's locally reversible update depends on the alphabet point above, which the sources disagree about.

events.what_happened: Kari, 'Reversible cellular automata', Developments in Language Theory (DLT 2005), LNCS 3572 (DOI 10.1007/11505877_5). I did not open it: Springer gave only a preview and the DOI redirected to a login. A search summary describes it as a short survey whose final section discusses local versus global reversibility. Wikipedia's reversible CA article attaches the statement that the question 'remains open for dimensions higher than two' to Kari 2005 together with Kari 2009. The page range differs by source: Wikipedia gives pp. 2–23; a DBLP listing as relayed by search gives pp. 57–68.
events.delivers: Not read. Per Wikipedia's citation attachment only: a survey statement that the question is open for dimensions above two.
events.direction: Not read. Cited by Wikipedia for the statement that the question is open above two. If correct, it is a post-2001 statement by Kari that the question remains open after the Durand-Lose result.

events.what_happened: Miller and Fredkin, 'Two-state, Reversible, Universal Cellular Automata in Three Dimensions', arXiv nlin/0501022 (v1 11 Jan 2005; v2 1 Feb 2005; v3 5 May 2005; ACM Computing Frontiers 2005 reversible computing workshop). Abstract (opened): 'A novel two-state, Reversible Cellular Automata (RCA) is described. This three-dimensional RCA is shown to be capable of universal computation. Additionally, evidence is offered that this RCA is capable of universal construction.' The abstract does not give the rule and does not mention partitioning. A search summary of a cell-auto.com page (not opened) describes a spatio-temporal partitioning scheme.
events.revisions: v1 11 Jan 2005; v2 1 Feb 2005; v3 5 May 2005 (current).
events.delivers: One specific two-state reversible CA in three dimensions that is universal. Does not address whether every reversible CA in d ≥ 3 is locally reversible.
events.direction: Not a confirming or refuting instance of the general question. It is a particular 3D RCA that was not checked for local reversibility.
events.object: A two-state three-dimensional reversible CA, rule not given in the abstract, shown capable of universal computation. Not checked for whether its rule is locally reversible.

events.what_happened: Kari, 'Structure of reversible cellular automata', Unconventional Computation (UC 2009), LNCS 5715 (DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-03745-0_5), as cited in Wikipedia's reversible CA article. I could not confirm the paper's existence from search, and the Springer chapter page redirected to a login. Per Wikipedia it is cited, with Kari 2005, for the statement that the question remains open for dimensions higher than two.
events.delivers: Not read. Existence and content known only from Wikipedia's citation.
events.direction: Not read. Cited by Wikipedia for the statement that the question is open above two.

events.what_happened: Eppstein, 'The Complexity of Iterated Reversible Computation', arXiv 2112.11607 (v1 22 Dec 2021; v2 7 Feb 2022; v3 21 Aug 2022; v4 21 Sep 2023; v5 18 Dec 2023); TheoretiCS 2 (2023), theoretics:9072. The paper is a complexity result and does not address the problem. Its Section 5 introduction (opened in the arXiv HTML v5) states: 'Every one-dimensional or two-dimensional reversible cellular automaton can be defined by a rule with locally reversible steps, as would be obtained by an array of reversible gates, but for higher dimensions this remains unknown.' It cites a reference [27] for this. I read v5; I did not confirm that the sentence is in v1.
events.revisions: v1 22 Dec 2021; v2 7 Feb 2022; v3 21 Aug 2022; v4 21 Sep 2023; v5 18 Dec 2023; journal version TheoretiCS 2023.
events.delivers: None. A status statement by an expert author that the d ≥ 3 case is open, with no result attached.
events.direction: Status statement only: open for d ≥ 3, in its own words. It cuts neither way.

events.what_happened: Arrighi and Nesme, 'The Block Neighborhood', arXiv 1012.1334 (v1 only, 3 Dec 2010; Journées Automates Cellulaires 2010, Turku). The abstract (opened) concerns the block neighbourhood of a reversible CA, related to its decomposition into a product of block permutations. The Introduction (opened via the arXiv HTML and ar5iv versions) states: 'It is always possible, by increasing the size of the alphabet, to simulate a d-dimensional CA by a reversible block CA of depth at most d+1.' It then says: 'In the case of dimensions 1 and 2, up to shifts, no additional space and no coding is needed; it is still an open problem whether the same can be said in higher dimensions.' It attributes the simulation results to Kari (1996, 1999) and Durand-Lose (2001).
events.delivers: Restates known results. Depth-(d+1) block simulation in every d, with enlarged alphabet. The exact version, with no extra space and no coding, is established for d = 1 and 2 only. Adds no new result for d ≥ 3.
events.remains: For d ≥ 3, the no-extra-space, no-coding version of the block representation, which the authors call open. Whether that is the statement's question is for the judging pass.
events.direction: Status statement: the no-extra-space form in d ≥ 3 is open, per the authors. Cuts neither way on the problem as worded.

events.what_happened: Arrighi and Nesme, 'A simple block representation of reversible cellular automata with time-symmetry', arXiv 1201.5529 (submitted 26 Jan 2012; Automata 2011 workshop, 6 pp.). Abstract (opened): 'we provide a very simple proof of the existence of a reversible circuit description implementing G', where G is the global evolution, and the description is time-symmetric. A broad class of time-symmetric CA admits an exact block representation that does not increase the state space. The abstract does not state the dimension scope of the general circuit result. A search summary of the full text (not readable through my tools) says the general construction uses auxiliary space, which is what would keep it outside the no-extra-space question for d ≥ 3. I could not verify that.
events.delivers: From the abstract: a shorter proof that a reversible circuit realises the global map of a reversible CA. Exact state-preserving block representation only for a class of time-symmetric CA. Dimension scope and whether the general circuit uses extra space are not settled from what I could read.
events.remains: The exact, no-extra-space form for general reversible CA in d ≥ 3, which the 2010 authors called open.
events.direction: Abstract cuts toward yes for a circuit description, with exact representation restricted to time-symmetric CA. Not a clear answer to the d ≥ 3 question.

events.what_happened: 'Two Graphs: Resolving the Periodic Reversibility of One-dimensional Finite Cellular Automata', arXiv 2402.05404 (nlin.CG, cs.CC; v1 8 Feb 2024; v2 27 Jul 2024; journal DOI 10.1016/j.amc.2024.129151 as linked from the abstract page). Abstract (opened): reversibility of one-dimensional finite CA is periodic in the number of cells, and a method computes the reversibility sequence. Authors not captured from my fetch. This is a neighbouring problem (1D, finite configurations, global reversibility). Discounted.
events.delivers: Periodicity of reversibility in cell count for 1D finite CA. Not about dimension ≥ 3 and not about local reversibility.
events.direction: Not on point: a 1D result on a neighbouring question.

events.what_happened: Haugland and Omland, 'New classes of reversible cellular automata', arXiv 2411.00721 (submitted 1 Nov 2024; single version). Abstract (opened): Boolean functions on k bits induce shift-invariant maps on n bits for n ≥ k; 'proper liftings' (bijective for every n) are exactly the local rules of reversible CA; the authors build new families for arbitrary k and ask whether all have been found for k ≤ 6. The framing is one-dimensional. Discounted: 1D, and about a family of rules rather than local reversibility in d ≥ 3.
events.delivers: New one-dimensional families of local rules of reversible CA (proper liftings). Not about d ≥ 3.
events.direction: Not on point: 1D, families of rules.

events.what_happened: Baby C. J. and Kamalika Bhattacharjee, 'Algebraic Characterization of Reversible First Degree Cellular Automata over Z_d', arXiv 2603.05253 (5 Mar 2026; cs.FL, cs.DM). Abstract (opened): three algebraic conditions decide whether a one-dimensional, three-neighbourhood, d-state CA with null boundary is reversible for every number of cells. Discounted: 1D, global reversibility only.
events.delivers: Global reversibility of 1D first-degree finite CA with null boundary. Not about d ≥ 3 or local reversibility.

events.what_happened: Maryia Kapytka, 'Lower Bounds on Inverse Cellular Automata via Proof Complexity', arXiv 2604.01041 (v1, 1 Apr 2026). Abstract (opened, summarised by the fetch tool): deciding injectivity of CA on bounded-size configurations is co-NP-complete (attributed to a theorem of Durand); the paper gives a direct reduction from UNSAT, a formalisation in bounded arithmetic V⁰, and proof-size lower bounds. The dimension is not stated in what I read. Discounted: a complexity result on a neighbouring question.
events.delivers: Complexity of testing injectivity of inverse CA on bounded configurations. No statement about local reversibility or about dimension ≥ 3.

events.what_happened: Jiang Yang, 'A Reversibility Characterization of Locally Finite Groups by Cellular Automata', arXiv 2606.29958 (submitted 29 Jun 2026). Abstract (opened, key sentences): 'A group G is locally finite if and only if, over every alphabet, every bijective cellular automaton A^G→A^G is reversible.' The paper says its counterexample is already on a countable alphabet and that it answers an open problem (its 'Open Problem 2'). Discounted: the CA are over arbitrary (infinite) alphabets, where bijective does not imply reversible; for finite-state CA on Z^d, bijective implies reversible, so this does not touch the problem as stated.
events.delivers: Over arbitrary alphabets, a characterisation of groups for which bijective CA are reversible. Not about local reversibility and not about finite-state CA in d ≥ 3.
events.direction: Not on point: a neighbouring problem about infinite alphabets.

events.what_happened: Alonso Castillo-Ramírez, 'A characterization of the reversibility of linear cellular automata', arXiv 2608.20600 (submitted 20 Aug 2026; single version; math.GR, cs.FL, math.DS). Abstract (opened): for a group G, field K and K-vector space V, a bijective linear CA V^G→V^G whose inverse is not a CA exists if and only if G is not locally finite and dim V ≥ |K|^ℵ₀; the paper says it answers an open problem of Ceccherini-Silberstein and Coornaert. The authors' AI declaration (opened in the arXiv HTML) is quoted under ai. Discounted: a neighbouring problem about linear CA over groups, not about d ≥ 3 or finite-state local reversibility.
events.delivers: For linear CA over arbitrary groups and infinite-dimensional V: a bijective linear CA with non-CA inverse exists iff G is not locally finite and dim V ≥ |K|^ℵ₀. Not about Z^d with d ≥ 3 and not about finite-state CA.
events.direction: Not on point: linear CA over groups.

disputes.summary: Wikipedia's reversible CA article says Durand-Lose (2001) showed that any reversible CA 'could be simulated by a (possibly different) locally reversible cellular automaton', and that the question 'remains open for dimensions higher than two'. Durand-Lose's abstract instead says every d-dimensional reversible CA 'can be expressed as the composition of d+1 block permutations', for all d, and that this proves the Toffoli–Margolus 1990 conjecture. These are not the same claim: one is a simulation, the other an exact expression.

Arrighi and Nesme (2010) say the depth-(d+1) block simulation of Durand-Lose uses 'increasing the size of the alphabet', and that the form with no extra space and no coding is known for d = 1, 2 and open for d ≥ 3. Wikipedia's block CA article says any reversible CA is simulated by a reversible block CA 'with a larger number of states'. The Durand-Lose abstract does not say whether its composition keeps the state set, so the sources do not settle which form the d ≥ 3 question asks for.

summary: Searches (at least 30, verbatim list below) found no event dated after 26 January 2024 that bears on the d ≥ 3 question. The Wikipedia article for the reversible CA topic, which the list entry links to, still reads on 12 October 2026: 'the question of whether every reversible transition function is locally reversible remains open for dimensions higher than two', with an unsolved-problem box asking whether every three-dimensional reversible CA is locally reversible. The list entry links to the reversible CA article, and I found no separate article for this question. The historical record is as follows. Toffoli and Margolus (1990) posed the question. Kari (1996) answered it positively for d = 1 and 2 (secondary descriptions, since Kari's paper was not reachable). Kari (1999, per an unopened search summary) bounded the layer count by d+1 in every dimension. Durand-Lose (2001) states in its abstract that every d-dimensional reversible CA is a composition of d+1 block permutations, for all d, and calls this a proof of the 1990 conjecture. Arrighi and Nesme (2010) say the depth-(d+1) block representation is known with enlarged alphabet, that the no-extra-space version holds for d = 1, 2 'up to shifts', and that it 'is still an open problem' for higher dimensions. Eppstein (arXiv 2112.11607, v5 Dec 2023) states that for higher dimensions 'this remains unknown'. Wikipedia attributes the open status to Kari 2005 and Kari 2009, both of which postdate Durand-Lose 2001 and which I could not read. The live disagreement is therefore whether Durand-Lose's composition is the locally reversible update the question asks about. If it preserves the automaton's state set and rule, the question looks answered for every d; if it needs more states, the no-extra-space form for d ≥ 3 remains open, which is what Arrighi and Nesme and Wikipedia say. I could not read the Durand-Lose body to decide. The in-window items are all neighbouring problems (1D finite CA, 1D liftings, 1D first-degree CA, bounded-configuration injectivity complexity, bijective CA over infinite alphabets, and linear CA over groups) and none addresses dimension three or higher or local reversibility. AI search: I searched for AI involvement with this problem and its reversible-CA area through lab announcements, AI-math trackers, Lean/Mathlib, and arXiv AI declarations. No AI system is named in connection with this question in any source. The only AI-declared item in the area is arXiv 2608.20600 (Castillo-Ramírez, Aug 2026), which declares use of 'OpenAI's ChatGPT 5.6 Sol' 'to assist with mathematical exploration and exposition'. It is about linear CA over groups, not this problem, and the declaration is not load-bearing, so I have not listed it in ai.systems for any event. The OpenAI unit-distance result (May 2026) and the DeepMind AlphaProof Nexus Erdős/OEIS results (search summaries) concern other problems; the Epoch FrontierMath open-problems overview names only the unit distance problem. Pre-2024 events were given none_found true by date and by what the sources name; for the in-window neighbouring papers I read abstracts and metadata only.
competing_reading: Reading that the question is already answered for every d: Durand-Lose's abstract says every d-dimensional reversible CA 'can be expressed as the composition of d+1 block permutations', for every d including d ≥ 3, and it claims to prove the 1990 Toffoli–Margolus conjecture. A block permutation is a fixed permutation applied to every block of a partition, which is a locally reversible step in the ordinary sense. Kari (1999, per an unopened summary) bounds the number of such layers by d+1 in every dimension. On this reading the Wikipedia 'open above two' sentence is stale or uses a stricter notion than the statement's words, and the statement is answered positively for all d. Reading that the question is open: Arrighi and Nesme (2010) say the depth-(d+1) block representation needs an enlarged alphabet, and that the no-extra-space version for d ≥ 3 is open. Wikipedia's block CA article says any reversible CA is simulated by a block CA 'with a larger number of states'. Eppstein (2023) says 'this remains unknown'. Wikipedia attaches the open statement to Kari 2005 and 2009, which postdate Durand-Lose, so Kari apparently did not treat the 2001 result as settling it. On this reading the judging pass should not count the 2001 composition as the locally reversible update of the same automaton.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Durand-Lose 2001 (DMTCS AA, pp. 145–154): the definition of block permutation; whether the composition is an equality of the same automaton's global map on the same alphabet and neighbourhood, or a simulation; whether shifts are absorbed into the permutation. (2) The full text of Kari 1999 (Fundamenta Informaticae 38): whether the d+1 layers act on the given alphabet and are the same automaton's rule, and what it says for d ≥ 3. (3) The exact sentences in Kari 2005 (DLT) and Kari 2009 (UC) that Wikipedia attaches to the open status, and whether they say 'locally reversible' or 'no extra space'. (4) Toffoli and Margolus (1990), for the wording of the original question. (5) A post-2024 paper, if one exists, that either proves or refutes the no-extra-space version for d ≥ 3, or that restates the d ≥ 3 question as open while citing Durand-Lose; none was found.

judgement.why: Every event after the snapshot is about a neighbouring question: 1D finite CA, 1D liftings, injectivity complexity, infinite alphabets, linear CA over groups. All are variant. The one close call is Durand-Lose 2001, which says in its abstract that it expresses every d-dimensional reversible CA as d+1 block permutations. Arrighi and Nesme (2010) say that construction enlarges the alphabet. Wikipedia's block CA article says it uses more states. Kari (2005, 2009, as cited by Wikipedia), Arrighi–Nesme and Eppstein all still call the d≥3 question open after 2001. So I read it as simulation by a different automaton, which is a changed question (variant), not as making the given automaton locally reversible (whole). Had I scored it whole, the problem would read open_stale rather than open. Kari 1996 settles only d=1 and 2, which the statement (d≥3) excludes, so it is variant. Kari 1999 is likewise an embedding/layer result, which I answered variant. The 2608.20600 AI declaration is not in ai.systems and concerns another problem, so its AI role is none.
judgement.doubts: The Durand-Lose body was never read, so the enlarged-alphabet reading rests on secondary sources. They agree with each other, and expert status statements after 2001 support them. 'Locally reversible' is undefined in the statement. For the old journal papers, verification was set to digested on the basis of journal publication.
